speaker: Zach Perret
title: How Plaid Survived on K Before Becoming Fintech Infrastructure | Zach Perret
question: In fintech, how does a rapid shift from low to high interest rates affect underlying infrastructure providers compared to consumer-facing apps?
guest: People were stuck at home using fintech like crazy, our customers were growing incredibly well, lots of new startups launching, lots of funding coming into the space. Then in the second half of twenty-two, interest rates went up, and our customers didn't quite know how to handle a higher interest rate environment. So we saw slower growth, though we were still growing through that period. I feel really proud of the resiliency of our business going through a really low to a moderately high interest rate environment quickly and still growing through it. But our customers had to retool. Our lenders that were used to making ZIRP-style loans now had to make higher-interest loans. A lot of the investing companies we worked with had to build products much more focused on savings and giving consumers the ability to buy treasuries, as opposed to purely buying stocks because stocks weren't growing as well. So a lot of retooling happened in our customer base, which lasted about six months, and then we returned to normal growth on a much higher base.

points.core: Rapid rate hikes force vertical fintech apps to retool their core products.
points.note: Accept: consumer fintechs pivoting product lines (e.g., equities to savings/treasuries, or low-rate loans to higher-interest lending). Do not credit: generic macro statements that higher rates hurt startups or funding.

points.core: Customer product retooling temporarily slows infrastructure growth for roughly half a year.
points.note: Accept: temporary growth deceleration lasting roughly one to two quarters (or several months) while downstream customers adapt. Do not credit: claiming infrastructure revenue collapses permanently or is completely unaffected.

points.core: Horizontal fintech infrastructure keeps growing through rate shocks despite customer-level disruption.
points.note: Accept: underlying plumbing staying resilient and resuming normal growth on a higher base once customers finish retooling. Do not credit: generic claims that B2B is safer than B2C without linking to rate-cycle resilience.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
A rapid rate spike tends to hit both layers, but through different channels and with different timing.

Consumer-facing apps feel it first and most directly. Lenders and BNPL providers see funding costs jump faster than they can reprice loans, credit losses rise, and loan demand falls; mortgage and refinancing-driven businesses can lose most of their volume. Customer acquisition gets harder as venture funding dries up and valuations compress. The exception is apps holding customer deposits or cash balances: neobanks and brokerages suddenly earn substantial net interest income on float, which helped several (such as Robinhood, Nubank and Revolut) reach profitability in 2022–2023.

Infrastructure providers (banking-as-a-service, payment processors, card issuing, data APIs) are hit second-order. Their revenue is usage- or volume-based, so they suffer as fintech clients shrink, consolidate or fail, and as startup formation slows. Those concentrated in startup customers are most exposed, while diversified ones with enterprise clients are more resilient. Some also benefit from float on held balances. However, stress exposes structural weaknesses: partner banks face deposit flight and regulatory scrutiny, and failures like Synapse's show infrastructure collapses can cascade to many apps at once.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
A rapid surge in interest rates hits consumer-facing fintechs immediately, whereas underlying infrastructure providers experience a cushioned, delayed impact. Consumer apps face an abrupt squeeze on unit economics: digital lenders see wholesale funding costs and borrower defaults spike, retail trading apps lose speculative volume, and venture-subsidized customer acquisition dries up. Although deposit-holding neobanks benefit from higher yields on reserves, fierce competition forces them to pass most of that interest to customers through high-yield accounts to prevent deposit flight.

Infrastructure providers, such as payment processors, data aggregators, and banking-as-a-service platforms, are initially insulated by multiyear contracts, high switching costs, and recurring software minimums. Many even capture an immediate windfall from interest earned on settlement float and custodial balances. Still, their usage-based revenues ultimately depend on downstream transaction volume. As consumer fintech clients curtail lending, consolidate, or fail, and as sponsor banks tighten balance-sheet and compliance requirements, infrastructure providers face lagged growth deceleration and churn, pushing them to pivot away from venture-backed startups toward established enterprise clients.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
A rapid move from low to high rates usually hurts consumer-facing apps more directly, while infrastructure providers see mixed and often partly offsetting effects.

Consumer apps take the hit on several fronts. Lenders and BNPL firms such as Affirm see funding costs rise faster than they can reprice loans, so margins shrink. Venture funding dries up as higher discount rates cut growth valuations, as happened in 2022–23. Growth paid for with heavy customer-acquisition spending becomes hard to sustain, and pressure to become profitable leads to layoffs, shutdowns, or consolidation. Neobanks are a partial exception because they earn more on the deposits they hold.

Infrastructure providers, such as payment processors, banking-as-a-service platforms, card issuers, and sponsor banks, often benefit at first because they earn interest on customer balances and funds in transit. Their B2B revenue is also stickier and less dependent on marketing spend. The downside is that they depend on their clients: when fintech customers fail or shrink, transaction volumes fall, and weak partners expose them to risk. Synapse's 2024 collapse and stricter regulation of sponsor banks are examples. In the end, the infrastructure layer is more resilient but not immune.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: A rapid jump from low to high interest rates hits consumer-facing fintech apps immediately and directly, while affecting underlying infrastructure providers more slowly through second-order pressures. Consumer apps—such as digital lenders, buy-now-pay-later platforms, and retail brokerages—face surging borrowing costs, rising credit delinquencies, and weaker demand for discretionary spending or speculative investing. While deposit-holding neobanks can temporarily earn higher net interest income on customer balances, intensifying competition quickly forces them to pass higher yields back to users, compressing margins. Meanwhile, infrastructure providers—covering payment processing, card issuing, banking-as-a-service, and identity verification—are better insulated initially because they avoid direct balance-sheet credit risk and rely on sticky, recurring API or volume-based fees with high switching costs. Still, they are not immune: as funding tightens and weaker consumer apps retrench or shut down, infrastructure firms experience longer enterprise sales cycles, slower transaction volume growth, customer churn, and heightened regulatory scrutiny over partner-bank compliance.
